results.title: Speculative Decoding and the Curse of Multilinguality
results.abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular technique for large language model (LLM) inference, enabling faster generation by drafting multiple tokens with a smaller draft model. However, the effectiveness of speculative decoding has mainly been studied for English. Motivated by the curse of multilinguality, we hypothesize that speculative decoding is far less effective for low-resource languages due to the limited multilingual capacities of smaller models. We test eleven languages under a standard speculative decoding setup and find strong evidence for our hypothesis. Next, we try to improve the multilingual capabilities of the smaller draft model via distillation from the larger model. We find, though, that distillation generalizes poorly across tasks in the same language, and we argue that assembling a task-agnostic, fully representative dataset is infeasible for low-resource languages. Finally, we propose weaker n-gram models as draft models; these provide moderate speed-ups due to their minuscule inference cost.

results.title: Mitigating Cold Starts in Container-Ephemeral Large Language Model Serving
results.venue: International Workshop on Quality of Service
results.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in serverless environments to enable elastic and costefficient inference. Existing LLM serving systems primarily optimize steady-state throughput under persistent GPU workers with long-lived model residency. In contrast, container-ephemeral deployments provision isolated instances on demand, causing high cold start latency during scale up events. In this paper, we present FaLLServe, a framework for container-ephemeral LLM serving in serverless environments. Our key insight is that the high cold start latency is dominated by the local deployment phase, particularly workflow overhead and tensor copy during model loading. FaLLServe introduces an initless model loading mechanism, an advanced container workflow, and a multi-level prewarm scheduler to reduce both cold start latency and its frequency. Experimental results show that FaLLServe reduces cold start latency by up to 49.$\times$ and improves tail latency by up to 270.3$\times$ under real-world workloads, making latency-critical LLM inference practical in ephemeral serving environments.

results.title: Direct GPU Energy Measurements of Batch-Level Sharing in Mixture-of-Experts and Recurrent Models
results.abstract: Energy claims for efficient neural networks are often inferred from operation counts. We report direct GPU energy measurements on two workloads that batch very differently, recurrent policies in GPU-vectorised multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, and ask one question of both: can the rows of a batch be made to share computation, across the batch and over time, at a measured saving? On recurrent policies the answer so far is no. Shared activity patterns exist but rarely last one step, masking a frozen policy fails, and trained-in masks succeed only because a fixed mask is equivalent to a narrow GRU, at 11x the energy of a small dense policy in our implementation. Test-time steering adds nothing beyond re-picking on either workload. On MoE models the answer is yes, and granularity decides how much: on Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware routing reads 25-31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05, with benchmark changes within noise at 500 items, and uses 12-18% less energy per token on a fused forward. We also introduce persistence-aware OEA, a one-parameter rule that keeps the batch-aware cut with about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch 32-64, though its energy has not yet been measured. These are pilot measurements on one GPU type, and we state their limits.
